entries.topic: The Scofield Reference Bible: 1909 OUP edition, 1917 revision, 1967 New Scofield, sales

claims.text: The Scofield Reference Bible first appeared in 1909, published by Oxford University Press; Scofield revised it in 1917; the 1917 edition 'attempts to date events of the Bible' and drew attention to Ussher's 4004 BC creation date and the gap theory (Mangum & Sweetnam p. 97).

The title page listed seven consulting editors: Henry G. Weston, James M. Gray, W. J. Erdman, A. T. Pierson, W. G. Moorehead, Elmore Harris, A. C. Gaebelein. Sandeen (1970 p. 224): 'Apparently Scofield only meant to acknowledge their assistance', though some speculated he sought support from both sides of the millenarian movement.
Sales exceeded two million copies by the end of the Second World War (Gaebelein 1943 p. 11).

Dunlap, citing Gaebelein: within 30 years OUP reported 1,925,000 copies published; Henry Frowde, an Oxford publisher in Brethren fellowship, advised Scofield that Oxford was the only house able to handle the work; OUP published 1909, revised editions 1917 and 1967.
Transcend Media Service, quoted by Check Your Fact: 'Frowde coordinated publication of The Scofield Reference Bible with John Armstrong in New York, head of the American branch of the Oxford Press.'
The Library of Congress copy of the 1917 edition carries the imprint New York, Oxford University Press, American Branch; London, H. Milford.
The 1917 notes are now in the public domain; the 1917 edition has been the best-selling Scofield edition in the UK and Ireland.
The 1967 revision (OUP) slightly modernized the KJV text and softened some of Scofield's positions; the note on John 1:17 was rewritten to seem to say the opposite (Campbell 2010).

Christianity Today, 14 April 1967: revision committee E. Schuyler English, Frank E. Gaebelein, William Culbertson, Charles L. Feinberg, Allan A. MacRae, Clarence E. Mason, Alva J. McClain, Wilbur M. Smith, John F. Walvoord; archaic words replaced; Ussher dating dropped; seven dispensations largely intact, sixth renamed from Grace to Church; Israel/Church distinction maintained; pre-tribulational premillennial view unchanged; note implying salvation by works removed; new note rejects the Anglo-Israel 'lost tribes' theory; the original 'has sold more copies than any other title issued by that press in the States'; 'several million copies in print'.

The claim that the 1917 edition incorporated references to the Balfour Declaration (2 Nov 1917) has no source: the Wikipedia page cited for it does not mention Balfour, and the 1917 notes checked (Gen 12, Gen 15, Deut 30, Ezek 38, Rom 11) contain no such reference and still describe Israel as 'now in the third dispersion'. Dropped as unsupported.

entries.topic: What the 1917 Scofield notes say about Israel, the land and the nations

claims.text: Gen 12:1 note: 'The Fourth Dispensation: Promise'; the Abrahamic Covenant 'wholly gracious and unconditional'; the dispensation 'was exclusively Israelitish'.

Gen 15:18 note: on 'curse him that curseth thee': 'Wonderfully fulfilled in the history of the dispersion. It has invariably fared ill with the people who have persecuted the Jew -- well with those who have protected him.' 'The gift of the land is modified by prophecies of three dispossessions and restorations'; 'Israel is now in the third dispersion, from which she will be restored ... at the return of the Lord as King under the Davidic Covenant'.

Deut 30:3 note: 'The Palestinian Covenant gives the conditions under which Israel entered the land of promise'; seven parts in order: (1) Dispersion for disobedience, (2) future repentance in the dispersion, (3) The return of the Lord, (4) Restoration to the land, (5) National conversion, (6) The judgment of Israel's oppressors, (7) National prosperity; 'the nation has never as yet taken the land under the unconditional Abrahamic Covenant, nor has it ever possessed the whole land'. In this sequence restoration follows the Lord's return.

Ezek 38:2 note: 'That the primary reference is to the northern (European) powers, headed up by Russia, all agree'; 'Meshech and Tubal (Moscow and Tobolsk)'; 'Russia and the northern powers have been the latest persecutors of dispersed Israel'; destruction to fall 'at the climax of the last mad attempt to exterminate the remnant of Israel in Jerusalem'; belongs to the future 'day of Jehovah' and Armageddon.

Rom 11 notes: 'That Israel has not been forever set aside is the theme of this chapter'; 'That the Christian now inherits the distinctive Jewish promises is not taught in Scripture'; 'During the great tribulation, a remnant out of all Israel will turn to Jesus as Messiah'; at 11:26 'Israel, regathered from all nations, restored to her own land and converted, is yet to have her greatest earthly exaltation and glory.'

Wikipedia: the Scofield Bible promotes dispensationalism (seven eras) and 'significantly influenced' Christian Zionism; quotes John Hagee: 'The man or nation that lifts a voice or hand against Israel invites the wrath of God.'
The 1967 revision kept the Israel/Church distinction and the pre-tribulational premillennial scheme.

entries.topic: Who paid for the Scofield Reference Bible; the Untermyer and Rothschild claims

claims.text: Dunlap: John Pirie (partner, Carson, Pirie and Scott, Chicago) and Alwyn Ball Jr. (New York real-estate broker, Southack and Ball) financially supported Scofield so he could devote time and facilities to the work; Francis Fitch, a printer, published the Scofield Bible Course in its early years; all three 'fellowshipped at so-called Brethren assemblies' in the New York area.

Rushing (2011), quoted by Check Your Fact: 'Though there were others in the conference circuit that contributed financially, Dr. Scofield acknowledged that Ball and Pirie made it possible for me to prepare' the Bible; Check Your Fact rated the Rothschild-funding claim false, 12 March 2025.

Scofield-Files, citing Gaebelein (1943) pp. 49-50: Alwyn Ball Jr., John T. Pirie, John B. Buss, Francis E. Fitch; Trumbull (1920) p. 75 names Pirie (as 'John C. Pirie'); Sandeen (1970) p. 191: Lyman Stewart gave $1,000 in 1908. Not checked against Sandeen directly.
Goeman (5 Oct 2024) names Ball (New York), Pirie (Chicago), Buss (St. Louis), Fitch (New York) and concludes the Zionist/Rothschild funding claim 'lacks credible evidence'.
Lyman Stewart (1840-1923) co-founded Union Oil of California and BIOLA (1908) and with his brother Milton contributed $300,000 to publish The Fundamentals.

Ó Cathail (WRMEA Oct 2015) asserts Scofield joined the 'Lotus' Club in 1901 with Untermeyer a committee member, quotes David W. Lutz that Untermyer used Scofield 'to inject Zionist ideas into American Protestantism' and that wealthy Zionists 'promoted and funded' his career including European travel; cites only Lutz and Canfield, no pages; does not claim they paid for the Bible. Contradicts the Lotos membership book (entry 3 March 1900; proposer Fraser, seconder Elderkin; election committee White, Elderkin, Ives).

Michael Collins Piper wrote for American Free Press and The Spotlight, papers backed by Willis Carto 'noted for their antisemitic and White separatist' themes; ADL, Simon Wiesenthal Center and MEMRI described him as a promoter of antisemitic conspiracy theories and Holocaust denial; The High Priests of War (2004) published by American Free Press.
Scofield-Files: Piper's 2004 book is the first known claim that the Rothschilds funded Scofield; Untermyer became president of Keren Hayesod in 1921.

Mike Rothschild (17 Jul 2024): 'The Rothschilds don't own Oxford University Press – the University of Oxford does'; finds no primary source connecting the Scofield Bible, Scofield or Darby to the family; traces a 2024 revival to John Rich on Tucker Carlson's show.

Timing against the Untermyer motive: Gaebelein, a consulting editor, wrote in 1905 that Zionism was 'a movement ... of unbelief', not the promised restoration; Untermyer's Keren Hayesod presidency began in 1921.
The Deut 30:3 note places 'Restoration to the land' after 'The return of the Lord', so the notes do not call for a Zionist programme before the Second Coming.
OUP's American branch published the edition as a commercial title (imprint).

claims.text: Audit re-fetch: Wikipedia states 'Sales of the Reference Bible exceeded two million copies by the end of World War II', footnoted to Gaebelein (1943) p. 11; Sandeen: 'Just what role these consulting editors played in the project has been the subject of some debate'; recent KJV Scofield Study Bible editions 'moved the textual changes made in 1967 to the margin' (no edition name or date given).

Audit re-fetch: CT 14 Apr 1967: 'hundreds of words' changed, 'marked by vertical lines'; Ussher abandoned and 'no dates are supplied for events prior to 2000 B.C.'; book introductions 'completely redone'; 2 Kings 17:23 note denies 'ten lost tribes'.

Audit re-fetch: Dunlap says Frowde was appointed Publisher to OUP in 1880 and 'fellowshiped all his adult life' with the Brethren; Pirie and Ball 'financially supported him'; Fitch's firm printed New York Stock Exchange lists; Scofield began work in 1903, first edition January 1909; Buss is not named by Dunlap.

Audit re-fetch: Scofield-Files quotes the 1999 CTRL-list document as saying Scofield 'was taken under the wing of Samuel Untermeier' and the 2002 Carlson article titled 'The Zionist-created Scofield bible'; it gives no source for Untermyer's 1921 Keren Hayesod presidency. Wikipedia's Untermyer entry says he 'served as president of the Keren Hayesod' without a year.
Audit re-fetch: Mike Rothschild paraphrases John Rich as saying Darby 'was connected to the Rothschilds'; no direct quote of Rich.
Audit re-fetch: Rom 11:1 note: Israel as a nation 'is yet to have its greatest exaltation as the earthly people of God'; Rom 11:5: remnant 'will become His witnesses after the removal of the church'.
